subsection.title: Learning Objectives
subsection.p: After completing this section, you should be able to:

list.item: Use De Morgan’s Laws to negate conjunctions and disjunctions.
Construct the negation of a conditional statement.
Use truth tables to evaluate De Morgan’s Laws.

subsection.title: Negation of Conjunctions and Disjunctions
subsection.p: In Chapter 1, Example 1.37 used a Venn diagram to prove De Morgan’s Law for set complement over union. Because the complement of a set is analogous to negation and union is analogous to an or statement, there are equivalent versions of De Morgan’s Laws for logic.

note.p: De Morgan’s Law for negation of a conjunction: $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q$$
De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a disjunction: $$\sim\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \land \right.\sim q$$
Negation of a conditional: $$\sim\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right) \equiv p \land \right.\sim q$$
Writing conditional as a disjunction: $$\left. p\rightarrow q \equiv \right.\sim p \vee q$$
Recall that the symbol for logical equivalence is: $$\equiv .$$

subsection.p: De Morgan’s Laws allow us to write the negation of conjunctions and disjunctions without using the phrase, “It is not the case that …” to indicate the parentheses. Avoiding this phrase often results in a written or verbal statement that is clearer or easier to understand.

problem.p: Write the negation of each statement in words without using the phrase, “It is not the case that.”

list.item: Kristin is a biomedical engineer and Thomas is a chemical engineer.
A person had cake or they had ice cream.

Kristin is a biomedical engineer and Thomas is a chemical engineer has the form “$$p \land q$$,” where $$p$$ is the statement, “Kristin is a biomedical engineer,” and $$q$$ is the statement, “Thomas is a chemical engineer.” By De Morgan’s Law, the negation of a conjunction, $$\sim(p \land q)$$, is logically equivalent to $$\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q.$$ $$\sim p$$ is “Kristen is not a biomedical engineer,” and $$\sim q$$ is “Thomas is not a chemical engineer.” By De Morgan’s Law, the solution has the form “$$\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q$$,” so the answer is: “Kristin is not a biomedical engineer or Tom is not a chemical engineer.”

A person had cake or they had ice cream has the form “$$p \vee q,$$” where $$p$$ is the statement, “A person had cake,” and $$q$$ is the statement, “A person had ice cream.” By De Morgan’s Law for the negations of a disjunction, $$\sim\left. (p \vee q) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \land \right.\sim q.$$ The solution is the statement: “A person did not have cake and they did not have ice cream.”

note.p: Jackie played softball or she ran track.
Brandon studied for his certification exam, and he passed his exam.

subsection.title: Negation of a Conditional Statement
subsection.p: The negation of any statement has the opposite truth values of the original statement. The negation of a conditional, $$\left. \sim(p\rightarrow q) \right.$$, is the conjunction of $$p$$ and not $$q$$, $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q.$$ Consider the truth table below for the negation of the conditional.

The only time the negation of the conditional statement is true is when $$p$$ is true, and $$q$$ is false. This means that $$\sim\left( p\rightarrow q \right)$$ is logically equivalent to $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q,$$ as the following truth table demonstrates.

problem.p: Write the negation of each conditional statement.

list.item: If Adele won a Grammy, then she is a singer.
If Henrik Lundqvist played professional hockey, then he did not win the Stanley Cup.

The negation of the conditional statement, $$\left. p\rightarrow q, \right.$$ is the statement, $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q.$$ The hypothesis of the conditional statement is $$p$$: “Adele won a Grammy,” and conclusion of the conditional statement is $$q$$: “Adele is a singer.” The negation of the conclusion, $$\sim q$$, is the statement: “She is not a singer.” Therefore, the answer is $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q:$$ “Adele won a Grammy, and she is not a singer.”

The hypothesis is $$p$$: “Henrik Lundqvist played professional hockey,” and the conclusion of the conditional statement is $$q$$: “He did not win the Stanley Cup.” The negation of $$q$$ is the statement: “He won the Stanley Cup.” The negation of the conditional statement is equal to $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q:$$ “Henrick Lundqvist played professional hockey, and he won the Stanley Cup.”

note.p: If Edna Mode makes a new superhero costume, then it will not include a cape.
If I had pancakes for breakfast, then I used maple syrup.

problem.p: Write the negation of each conditional statement.

list.item: If all cats purr, then my partner’s cat purrs.
If a penguin is a bird, then some birds do not fly.

The negation of the conditional statement $$\left. p\rightarrow q\operatorname{} \right.$$ is the statement $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q.$$ The hypothesis of the conditional statement is $$p$$: “All cats purr,” and the conclusion of the conditional statement is $$q$$: “My partner’s cat purrs.” The negation of the conclusion, $$\sim q$$, is the statement: “My partner’s cat does not purr.” Therefore, the answer is $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q:$$ “All cats purr, but my partner’s cat does not purr.”

The hypothesis is $$p$$: “A penguin is a bird,” and the conclusion of the conditional statement is $$q$$: “Some birds do not fly.” The negation of $$q$$ is the statement: “All birds fly.” Therefore, the negation of the conditional statement is equal to $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q:$$ “A penguin is a bird, and all birds fly.”

note.p: If some people like ice cream, then ice cream makers will make a profit.
If Raquel cannot play video games, then nobody will play video games.

subsection.p: Many of the properties that hold true for number systems and sets also hold true for logical statements. The following table summarizes some of the most useful properties for analyzing and constructing logical arguments. These properties can be verified using a truth table.

problem.p: Write the negation of each conditional statement applying De Morgan’s Law.

list.item: If mom needs to buy chips, then Mike had friends over and Bob was hungry.
If Juan had pizza or Chris had wings, then dad watched the game.

The conditional has the form “If $$p$$ then $$q$$ or $$r$$,” where $$p$$ is “Mom needs to buy chips,” $$q$$ is “Mike had friends over,” and $$r$$ is “Bob was hungry.” The negation of $$\left. p\rightarrow(q \land r) \right.$$ is $$\left. p \land \right.\sim(q \land r).$$ Applying De Morgan’s Law to the statement $$\sim(q \land r)$$ the result is $$\sim\left. q \vee \right.\sim r$$, so our conditional statement becomes $$\left. p \land ( \right.\sim\left. q \vee \right.\sim r).$$ By the distributive property for conjunction over disjunction, this statement is equivalent to $$\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right) \vee \left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim r} \right).$$ Translating the statement $$\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right) \vee \left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim r} \right)$$ into words, the solution is: “Mom needs to buy chips and Mike did not have friends over, or Mom needs to buy chips and Bob was not hungry.”

The conditional has the form “If $$p$$ or $$q$$, then $$r$$,” where $$p$$ is “Juan had pizza,” $$q$$ is “Chris had wings,” and $$r$$ is “Dad watched the game.” The negation of $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right)\rightarrow r \right.$$ is $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right) \land \right.\sim r.$$ By the distributive property for disjunction over conjuction, the statement is equivalent to $$\left( {\left. p \vee \right.\sim r} \right) \land \left( {\left. q \vee \right.\sim r} \right).$$ Translating the statement $$\left( {\left. p \vee \right.\sim r} \right) \land \left( {\left. q \vee \right.\sim r} \right)$$ into words, the solution is: “Juan had pizza or dad did not watch the game, and Chris had wings or dad did not watch the game.”

note.p: If Eric needs to replace the light bulb, then Marcus left the light on all night or Dan broke the bulb.
If Trenton went to school and Regina went to work, then Merika cleaned the house.

subsection.title: Evaluating De Morgan’s Laws with Truth Tables
subsection.p: In Chapter 1, you learned that you could prove the validity of De Morgan’s Laws using Venn diagrams. Truth tables can also be used to prove that two statements are logically equivalent. If two statements are logically equivalent, you can use the form of the statement that is clearer or more persuasive when constructing a logical argument.

The next example will prove the validity of one of De Morgan’s Laws using a truth table. The same procedure can be applied to any two logical statement that you believe are equivalent. If the last column of the truth table is a tautology, then the two statements are logically equivalent.

problem.p: Construct a truth table to verify De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a conjunction, $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q$$, is valid.

solution.p: Step 1: To verify any logical equivalence, you must first replace the logical equivalence symbol, $$\equiv$$, with the biconditional symbol, $$\leftrightarrow$$. The statement $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q$$ becomes $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\leftrightarrow \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q.$$ Step 2: Next, you create a truth table for the statement. Because we have two basic statements, $$p$$, and $$q$$, the truth table will have four rows to account for all the possible outcomes. The columns will be $$p$$, $$q$$, $$\sim p$$, $$\sim q$$, $$p \land q,$$$$\sim(p \land q),$$$$\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q,$$ and the biconditional statement is $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\leftrightarrow \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q.$$

Step 3: Finally, verify that the statement is valid by confirming it is a tautology. In this instance, the last column is all true. Therefore, the statement is valid and De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a conjunction is verified.

note.p: Construct a truth table to verify De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a disjunction, $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p \vee q} \right) \equiv \text{\textasciitilde}p \land \text{\textasciitilde}q$$, is valid.

subsection.title: Check Your Understanding
subsection.p: De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a conjunction states that $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p \land q} \right)$$ is logically equivalent to ___________________.
De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a disjunction states that $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p \vee q} \right)$$ is logically equivalent to __________________.
The negation of the conditional statement, $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p\rightarrow q} \right)$$, is logically equivalent to _____________.

$$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p\rightarrow q} \right)} \right) \equiv p\rightarrow q$$, which means the conditional statement is logically equivalent to $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p \land \text{\textasciitilde}q} \right).$$ Apply _______________________ to the statement $$\text{\textasciitilde}\left( {p \land \text{\textasciitilde}q} \right)$$ to show that the conditional statement $$p\rightarrow q \equiv \text{\textasciitilde}p \vee q.$$

exercises.instruction: For the following exercises, write the negation of each conditional in words by applying the property for the negation of a conditional.

problem.p: If a student scores an 85 on the final exam, then they will receive an A in the class.
If a person does not pass their road test, then they will not receive their driver’s license.
If a student does not do their homework, then they will not play video games.
If a commuter misses the bus, then they will not go to work today.
If a racecar driver gets pulled over for speeding, then they will not make it to the track on time for the race.
If Rene Descartes was a philosopher, then he was not a mathematician.
If George Boole invented Boolean algebra and Thomas Edison invented the light bulb, then Pacman is not the best video game ever.
If Jonas Salk created the polio vaccine, then his child received the vaccine or his child had polio.
If Billie Holiday sang the blues or Cindy Lauper sang about true colors, then John Lennon was not a Beatle.
If Percy Jackson is the lightning thief and Artemis Fowl is a detective, then Artemis Fowl will catch Percy Jackson.
If all rock stars are men, then Pat Benatar is not a rock star.
If Lady Gaga is a rock star, then some rock stars are women.
If yellow combined with blue makes green, then all colors are beautiful.
If leopards have spots and zebras have stripes, then some animals are not monotone in color.
